Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines · Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

difficult adjective

of a person: hard to deal with

also awkward, uncooperative, being difficult, hard to get on with

classical

Mart. 12.46.1: difficilis facilis, jūcundus acerbus es īdem
Cic. Sen. 65: mōrōsī et anxiī et īrācundī et difficilēs senēs
Ter. Heaut. 535: hunc difficilem invītum servāret senem

difficilis, difficile

difficult, hard to manage, contrary

Of character, “hard to manage or to please, obstinate, morose” (Lewis & Short); its opposite is facilis, easy-going. To be difficult on purpose: difficilem ostendēs tē esse, “you’ll make a show of being difficult” (Ter. Heaut. 933).

Examples

  • difficilis facilis, jūcundus acerbus es īdem: nec tēcum possum vīvere, nec sine tē

    difficult and easy, sweet and sour, you are both at once: I can’t live with you, or without youMart. 12.46.1–2

  • at sunt mōrōsī et anxiī et īrācundī et difficilēs senēs. sī quaerimus, etiam avārī; sed haec mōrum vitia sunt, nōn senectūtis

    but old men are grumpy, anxious, irritable and difficult, and, if we look, miserly too; but these are faults of character, not of old ageCic. Sen. 65

  • tempore difficilēs veniunt ad arātra juvencī

    in time the stubborn bullocks come to the ploughOv. Ars 1.471

Other words

  • mōrōsus, mōrōsa, mōrōsum — hard to please, peevish

    also used · classical · Cic. Or. 104: difficilēs ac mōrōsī

See also difficult, grumpy, stubborn, irritable, particular.

SourcesLewis & Short: difficilis · Lewis & Short: morosus
